title: Basic knitted cowl
subtitle: A stocking-stitch tube worked in the round on 5 mm needles.
excerpt: A cowl knitted in the round in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles with worsted-weight yarn, finishing at 60 cm circumference and 25 cm tall. The tube is seamless and the stocking stitch face looks outward on the right side. A twisted 1x1 rib at the cast-on and bind-off edges keeps both openings from rolling.
sourceNotes: Seamless tubular cowls worked in the round draw on the knitting-in-the-round techniques documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), citations only. Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, documents circular-needle neckwear in tubular construction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A technique for working a small circumference in the round on one long circular needle (80 cm or longer) by pulling a loop of cable through the stitches at the halfway point, splitting them into two groups.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.
A bind-off that produces a looser, more elastic edge than the standard bind-off. K2tog through back loops, slip result back to left needle, repeat.

content.text: This is a seamless cowl knitted in the round in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, finishing at 60 cm circumference and 25 cm tall. Every round is a knit round and the stocking-stitch face sits on the outside of the tube automatically when knitting in the round. A short 1x1 twisted rib at each opening gives a firm edge that does not roll.

In-the-round construction was chosen because a seamless stocking-stitch tube needs no seam to close the join, and the stocking-stitch fabric would curl badly at the edges if worked flat without a border. The
magic loop

method on one long circular needle is the most flexible approach for a 60 cm circumference. The finished cowl needs about 200 m (approximately 110 g) of worsted-weight yarn and sits as a single loop around the neck, pulled up to the chin in cold weather.
What you need

items.name: Worsted-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any worsted-weight yarn. Wool gives the best warmth and drape for a cowl.

items.name: 5 mm circular needle, 80 cm or longer (UK 6 / US 8)
items.substitutions: A 60 cm circular works if you prefer; 80 cm is more comfortable for magic loop.

items.name: Stitch marker
items.substitutions: A loop of contrast yarn works.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch in the round on 5 mm needles, blocked. Gauge in the round can differ by up to one stitch per 10 cm from flat gauge on the same needle size because knitters typically throw the yarn differently when purling. Always swatch in the round. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished circumference by approximately 3.3 cm at this stitch count: 19 sts per 10 cm gives about 57 cm circumference; 17 sts per 10 cm gives about 63 cm. Round gauge drift across the 60 body rounds changes the finished height by up to 5 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit): right needle from left to right through front of stitch, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through. In the round, every round is all knit for stocking stitch.
P (purl): used in the rib sections only.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 108 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is a multiple of 2 for the rib edge. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 108 stitches: (15.7 x 108) / 10 + 15 = 169.6 + 15 = about 185 cm. Leave a tail of at least 185 cm; wind it loosely around your fingers or a small card before making the slip knot.

Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 108 stitches on the needle. Join to work in the round being careful not to twist the cast-on. Place a stitch marker to mark the beginning of the round.
Body
Rib section (8 rounds): *K1 tbl, P1; repeat from * to end. (108 sts) -- K tbl (knit through back loop) gives a slightly twisted knit stitch that firms up the rib edge.
Body (60 rounds): K all stitches every round. (108 sts)
Work the body until the cowl measures 23 cm from the cast-on edge (the rib section plus the body). At the halfway mark of the body (approximately round 30 of the 60 body rounds), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at round 30 of the body section you should have 108 stitches on the needle.
Closing rib section (8 rounds): *K1 tbl, P1; repeat from * to end. (108 sts)
Bind off
Stretchy bind-off

in rib pattern: work each stitch in pattern and use the K2tog-through-back-loops method: K2tog tbl, slip resulting stitch back to left needle, K2tog tbl, repeat to end. The stretchy bind-off keeps the top edge as open as the cast-on.
Common faults

Twisted cast-on join. When joining in the round after the cast-on, it is easy to allow one or two stitches to cross the join and twist the tube. Always lay the cast-on edge flat, confirm the stitches all face the same direction along the needle, before working the first joining round.

Visible jog at the round join. The jog is where each round ends and the next begins. In stocking stitch in the round the jog is a small stagger in the fabric. It is less visible in dark yarns. A slip-stitch join technique at the beginning of each round can minimise it: slip the first stitch of each new round before knitting the second.
Bound-off edge rolling or tighter than cast-on. The stretchy bind-off above should match the cast-on edge. If the bound-off edge is still narrower, rework it on a needle two sizes larger.
Finishing
Weave in both tails at the cast-on join and bind-off, running each tail in opposite directions around the inside of the rib for 5 to 6 stitches. Trim close.
Block by soaking in cool water, pressing out the water, and laying flat over a round foam blocking aid or a folded towel that fills the cowl tube so it dries in the round shape. Leave overnight.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat or over a rounded form to dry. Do not hang as the weight will stretch the tube lengthwise.
What to try next

The ribbed cowl works the full tube in rib rather than just the edges, giving a stretchier fit. The infinity cowl is the same tube worked to a longer height so it doubles around the neck. The lace cowl applies a simple lace pattern across the tube in the same basic in-the-round construction.
